issues.issue: The first clause is qualified "in all material respects" but the second warrants that "all information supplied by, on behalf of, or concerning the Mortgagor is true, accurate and complete" without any materiality or knowledge limit and without identifying whose information or supplied to whom. The reach of that unbounded second clause is the natural battleground for any loan-file misrepresentation claim.

The representation that "[t]he proceeds of the Revolving Credit Loan have been fully disbursed and there is no requirement for future advances thereunder" cannot be squared with Section 2(a), which sells "all additional balances resulting from related Draws," or with Section 7(xx), which warrants that every loan has a Draw Period of 5, 10 or 15 years. A revolving line by definition contemplates future advances.

This warrants that "upon recordation the Purchaser or its designee will be the owner of record of the Mortgage," while Sections 4(b) and 6(a) provide that assignments are recorded from the HELOC Seller to the Indenture Trustee, and 4(c) puts the Indenture Trustee's code on MERS. Who becomes owner of record is stated two different ways.

Compliance with predatory-lending and disclosure laws is warranted only "in all material respects," while Section 2.02(n) of the Insurance and Indemnity Agreement provides that a mortgagor's Truth-in-Lending claim conclusively constitutes notice of a breach of this Section 7 and that "[a]ny such breach shall be deemed material." The materiality qualifier here and the deeming provision there pull in opposite directions.

The same sentence warrants that the loan "is not delinquent in payment more than 29 days" and that "no payment has been 30 days delinquent during the preceding twelve month period." The two delinquency thresholds are stated one day apart and over different periods, leaving the permitted delinquency status uncertain.

The clause protects "the interests of the Trustee on behalf of the Noteholders and the Note Insurer" and requires modifications to be reflected in the "Revolving Credit Loan Schedule," but neither "the Trustee" (as against the Indenture Trustee or the Owner Trustee) nor the "Revolving Credit Loan Schedule" is a term defined in this Agreement. Both references have to be supplied from outside the words used.

The representation reaches only selection procedures "reasonably believed by the HELOC Seller to be adverse," making the seller's own belief the measure of the warranty. Adverse selection that EMC did not believe adverse would not breach it, a limit the surrounding absolute representations do not carry.

This permits a Mortgaged Property to be held "by leasehold for a term longer than the term of the related Mortgage," while Section 7(mm) requires that the remaining lease term not terminate less than ten years after the maturity date of the HELOC. The two provisions set different minimum lease terms for the same loans.

The clause addresses only "first lien" and "second lien" Revolving Credit Loans, although the transaction is defined throughout as covering "first and junior lien" HELOCs. On an expressio unius reading a third-lien or other junior-lien loan carries no security-agreement warranty at all.

The representation is introduced "with respect to each junior lien Revolving Credit Loan" but the operative promise runs only to "the mortgagee under the second lien Revolving Credit Loan." Whether junior liens other than second liens get the notice-and-cure protection is not resolved by the words used.

The mechanics'-lien exception is limited to liens "insured against by the title insurance policy referred to in (w) below," but clause (w) does not require a title policy for junior lien HELOCs that are Piggyback Loans of $200,000 or less. For those loans the carve-out has no referent.

"[T]o the best of the HELOC Seller's knowledge" is placed only before the litigation clause, leaving the statements about material damage, repair and condemnation absolute. Whether the knowledge qualifier reaches back over the earlier clauses of the same sentence is the classic question this drafting poses.

The junior-lien notice warranty applies only "where required or customary in the jurisdiction," a standard with no stated source and no benchmark for what is customary. Whether any given loan is covered by the representation cannot be determined from the provision.

The encroachment exception depends on the title insurance policy "referred to in clause (w) below," yet clause (w) excuses a policy entirely for junior lien Piggyback Loans of $200,000 or less and permits a mere lien search instead. For those loans the exception cross-references something that need not exist.

This warrants hazard insurance by an insurer "acceptable under the Fannie Mae Guides" and flood coverage meeting Federal Insurance Administration guidelines, while Section 7(z) warrants insurance from an insurer "acceptable to the HELOC Seller" in an amount measured by a different least-of-three flood formula. Two different insurance standards are warranted for the same properties.

The junior-lien title insurance carve-out turns on whether a loan is a "Piggyback Loan" with an initial principal amount of $200,000 or less, but "Piggyback Loan" is capitalized and defined nowhere in this Agreement. The class of loans excused from the title-policy requirement cannot be identified.

This requires an appraisal by a disinterested Qualified Appraiser satisfying Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Title XI of FIRREA, while Section 7(y) warrants only an appraisal "which conformed to the underwriting requirements of the originator." The two appraisal representations set different standards for the same file.

This warrants only that each appraisal "conformed to the underwriting requirements of the originator," whereas Section 7(x) warrants a Qualified Appraiser and compliance with FIRREA and the agency guides. Whether an originator-standard appraisal satisfies the pool's appraisal warranty depends on which clause controls.

This warrants insurance from "an insurer which is acceptable to the HELOC Seller" and flood coverage equal to the least of three amounts, while Section 7(v) requires an insurer acceptable under the Fannie Mae Guides and flood coverage meeting Federal Insurance Administration guidelines conforming to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac requirements. The same insurance is warranted twice on inconsistent terms.

Each HELOC is warranted to be a REMIC "qualified mortgage," but Section 2(a) sells lines of credit whose balances grow with post-closing Draws and Section 2.05(b) of the Sale and Servicing Agreement expressly contemplates discovery that a HELOC is not a qualified mortgage. The absolute warranty and the transaction's revolving structure sit uneasily together.

After a closed list of named statutes and labels, the clause sweeps in "a similarly classified loan using different terminology under a law imposing heightened regulatory scrutiny or additional legal liability." That catch-all has no boundary and would have to be read against the enumerated specifics that precede it.

The representation is made as to "Schedule A of the Prospectus Supplement," while this Agreement has its own Schedule A (Required Ratings for Each Class of Notes) and Section 5(d) refers to yet another Schedule A attached to the interim certification. Which Schedule A is warranted must be construed.

This fixes the Standard & Poor's LEVELS Glossary at "Version 5.6c, Appendix E, attached hereto as Exhibit 6," while Section 2.01(c)(v) of the Sale and Servicing Agreement identifies the very same Exhibit 6 to this Agreement as "Version 5.7 Revised." The two documents describe the same exhibit as two different versions of the test for a covered loan.

"[T]he underwriting guidelines of the related originator" are neither identified, attached, nor dated, and the clause admits no allowance for documented exceptions. What guidelines a loan had to satisfy is the central question in any origination-quality dispute and cannot be answered from the instrument.

Recordation is warranted "in accordance with the requirements of Section 2.01 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement," but Section 2.01(e) of that agreement requires assignments to be submitted for recording only upon a Recordation Event, whereas Section 6(a) of this Agreement imposes a flat 180-day recording deadline. The two recording regimes cannot both be the measure of this warranty.

The Mortgage File is warranted to contain the documents listed in Section 2.01 of the Sale and Servicing Agreement, while Section 1 of this Agreement defines the Mortgage File as the items referred to in Exhibit 1. The two lists are not identical, so the contents warranted depend on which definition governs.

This warrants that Minimum Monthly Payments "are due and payable on the first day of each month," while the Section 1 definition of Due Date makes the payment date whatever "the related Mortgage Note" specifies. The fixed first-of-the-month rule and the note-driven Due Date cannot both be right for every loan.

"Accepted Servicing Practices" is capitalized as a defined term but is not defined in this Agreement, and the servicing is performed under a separate Servicing Agreement not delivered with it. The standard against which servicing is warranted has to be found outside the instrument.

The clause turns on whether a loan is a "MERS Loan" recorded on the "MERS System," while Section 1 defines only the "MERS® System" and Section 4(c) speaks of HELOCs "registered on the MERS® System." It also warrants an Assignment acceptable for recording "other than with respect to the blank assignee," although Sections 4(b) and 6(a) contemplate assignments running to the Indenture Trustee.

The proviso that "no residence or dwelling is a single parcel of real property with a cooperative housing corporation erected thereon, or a mobile home" is garbled — a cooperative corporation is not something erected on a parcel — and it is unclear whether it excludes co-op units, co-op buildings, or neither. The mechanical defect changes what property types are warranted out of the pool.

The clause warrants that each prepayment penalty "is at least equal to the lesser of" the maximum permitted by law and six months' interest — a floor on the size of borrower penalties, where a purchaser protection would set a ceiling. Read literally it warrants that borrowers were charged the maximum lawful penalty, which cannot be reconciled with the predatory-lending compliance warranted in Section 7(e).

This requires that a lease not terminate less than ten years after the maturity date of the HELOC, while Section 7(zz)(ix) requires only that a ground lease term extend "at least five years beyond the maturity date of the related Revolving Credit Loan." A leasehold property can satisfy one and breach the other.

"[C]ustomary and enforceable provisions such as to render the rights and remedies of the holder thereof adequate" states no standard for what is customary or adequate and no jurisdiction by which to measure it. Whether a given mortgage form breaches the warranty is unanswerable on these words.

The exception for "any applicable security agreement or chattel mortgage referred to above" points back to Section 7(l), which addresses only first and second lien loans. For other junior lien loans the cross-reference has no content.

The warranty extends to any circumstance "that could reasonably be expected to cause investors to regard the Revolving Credit Loan as an unacceptable investment," without identifying which investors or what makes a loan unacceptable. That open-ended standard, unlike the specific bankruptcy statements beside it, has no boundary a court could apply without extrinsic evidence.

This warrants an adjustable "Mortgage Interest Rate" resetting monthly against an Index and Gross Margin, while Section 1 defines "Mortgage Rate" as "the annual rate of interest borne by a Mortgage Note" and builds Net Mortgage Rate on it. The Agreement uses two rate terms for the same loans without reconciling them.

"[E]ach Revolving Credit Loan requires the payment of a Cancellation Fee, where applicable" is self-cancelling: the qualifier "where applicable" removes any content from the warranty, and "Cancellation Fee" is nowhere defined. Nothing could breach it as written.

Every loan is warranted to have a term of 180 or 300 months and a Draw Period of 5, 10 or 15 years "followed by an Amortization Period of ten years." A 10-year Draw Period plus a 10-year Amortization Period is 240 months, which is neither of the two permitted terms, so the two sentences cannot both hold.

Clause (ix) requires the ground lease term to run "at least five years beyond the maturity date" of the loan, while Section 7(mm) requires that a lease not terminate less than ten years after maturity. The two leasehold warranties set incompatible minimum terms.
